title: Water, impurities and hardness
learn: Natural water is not chemically pure; its impurities depend on the source of water and on the materials with which it comes in contact.
Hardness is mainly associated with dissolved calcium and magnesium salts and is classified as temporary (carbonate) and permanent (non-carbonate) hardness.
For calculations, different hardness-producing salts are converted to a common calcium-carbonate-equivalent basis.

sections.heading: Introduction: natural water and its sources
paragraphs: The textbook begins by treating water as an essential natural material whose usefulness depends strongly on its quality. Naturally occurring water is seldom pure because, during its movement through air, soil and rock, it picks up gases, mineral matter, suspended solids and living organisms.

Natural sources are grouped as rain water, river water, lake water, spring water and well water. Rain water is comparatively pure when it first condenses, but it can absorb atmospheric gases and suspended impurities. River and lake water collect material from surface drainage and biological surroundings. Spring and well water remain in contact with underground mineral matter for longer periods and therefore commonly contain more dissolved salts.

Because the kind and amount of impurity vary with source, the same water may be suitable for one use and unsuitable for another. The chapter therefore examines the impurities first and then the treatment methods used to remove or control them.

book_refs.note: Introduction and natural sources of water

sections.heading: Impurities in natural water
paragraphs: The textbook classifies the impurities broadly as physical, chemical and biological. Physical impurities include suspended material that produces turbidity, colour, taste and odour. Chemical impurities include dissolved inorganic salts, dissolved gases and traces of organic substances. Biological impurities include algae, bacteria, fungi, viruses and other microscopic organisms.

Dissolved mineral salts are especially important in engineering use. Salts of calcium and magnesium are responsible for hardness; chlorides, sulphates and bicarbonates occur frequently in natural waters. Dissolved gases such as carbon dioxide and oxygen can influence corrosion and water quality, while biological contamination is important when the water is intended for drinking.
For Unit I, the main consequence of dissolved calcium and magnesium salts is hardness, so the textbook next defines hardness and distinguishes its two forms.

sections.heading: Hardness of water
paragraphs: Hardness is the property of water that prevents it from producing lather readily with soap. Instead of forming a stable lather, soap reacts with dissolved calcium and magnesium ions to form insoluble precipitates. The textbook therefore treats calcium and magnesium salts as the principal hardness-producing constituents.

Temporary hardness, also called carbonate hardness, is caused mainly by the bicarbonates of calcium and magnesium. It can be removed by boiling because the bicarbonates decompose to insoluble products.

Permanent hardness, also called non-carbonate hardness, is caused mainly by chlorides and sulphates of calcium and magnesium. These salts do not decompose simply by boiling, so permanent hardness requires a chemical softening or ion-exchange process.

sections.heading: Removal of temporary hardness by boiling
paragraphs: On boiling, soluble bicarbonates are converted into insoluble precipitates. Calcium bicarbonate gives calcium carbonate, whereas magnesium bicarbonate ultimately gives magnesium hydroxide. The precipitated solids can then be separated from the water.

sections.heading: Calcium-carbonate equivalents
paragraphs: A water sample may contain several different calcium and magnesium salts. Their concentrations cannot be added directly to obtain hardness because their molar masses and chemical equivalents differ. The textbook therefore converts the amount of every hardness-producing substance into the amount of calcium carbonate that would be chemically equivalent to it.

Calcium carbonate is used as the common reference because its molar mass is 100 and, for hardness reactions, its chemical equivalent is 50. Once each constituent is converted to a CaCO₃ equivalent, the individual contributions can be added directly.
formulas: \(\text{CaCO}_3\text{ equivalent}=\dfrac{\text{mass of hardness-producing substance}\times 50}{\text{chemical equivalent of hardness-producing substance}}\)

tables.caption: CaCO₃ conversion factors from textbook Table 1
headers: Factor for conversion to CaCO₃ equivalent

sections.heading: Units and degree of hardness
paragraphs: Hardness may be expressed in several units. The textbook gives parts per million, milligrams per litre, Clark degree, French degree and milliequivalents per litre, and also provides the relationships between them.

For dilute aqueous solutions, 1 mg of CaCO₃ equivalent per litre is numerically the same as 1 ppm. Clark degree is based on grains of CaCO₃ equivalent per gallon of water, whereas French degree represents one part of CaCO₃ equivalent in one hundred thousand parts of water.

self_checks.question: Why is hardness expressed as CaCO₃ equivalent?
self_checks.answer: It converts different hardness-producing salts to one common basis, making their contributions directly additive and comparable.

title: Hardness calculations and complexometric estimation
learn: Numerical hardness is obtained by converting every hardness-producing constituent to its CaCO₃ equivalent and adding the appropriate contributions.
The EDTA method is a complexometric method in which Ca²⁺ and Mg²⁺ form stable complexes with EDTA.
At about pH 10, Eriochrome Black T gives a wine-red metal–indicator complex; the end point is the change from wine red to distinct blue.
The textbook gives the complete procedure for total, permanent and temporary hardness by the EDTA method.

sections.heading: Numerical calculation of hardness from dissolved salts
paragraphs: When a water analysis gives the concentration of several dissolved salts, each hardness-producing salt is first multiplied by its CaCO₃ conversion factor. The CaCO₃-equivalent values are then grouped according to the type of hardness they produce.

Bicarbonates of calcium and magnesium contribute to temporary hardness. Chlorides and sulphates of calcium and magnesium contribute to permanent hardness. Total hardness is the sum of temporary and permanent hardness.

sections.heading: Worked example — temporary, permanent and total hardness
paragraphs: Textbook Example 4 uses a sample containing \(\mathrm{Mg(HCO_3)_2}=73\,mg/L\), \(\mathrm{Ca(HCO_3)_2}=162\,mg/L\), \(\mathrm{MgCl_2}=95\,mg/L\) and \(\mathrm{CaSO_4}=136\,mg/L\).

For \(\mathrm{Mg(HCO_3)_2}\), the CaCO₃ equivalent is \(73\times\dfrac{100}{146}=50\,mg/L\). For \(\mathrm{Ca(HCO_3)_2}\), it is \(162\times\dfrac{100}{162}=100\,mg/L\). Hence temporary hardness is \(150\,ppm\).

For \(\mathrm{MgCl_2}\), the CaCO₃ equivalent is \(95\times\dfrac{100}{95}=100\,mg/L\). For \(\mathrm{CaSO_4}\), it is \(136\times\dfrac{100}{136}=100\,mg/L\). Hence permanent hardness is \(200\,ppm\).
Therefore total hardness is \(150+200=350\,ppm\).

sections.heading: Principle of the EDTA complexometric method
paragraphs: The textbook identifies the EDTA method as a complexometric method. Ethylenediaminetetraacetic acid is used in the form of its disodium salt. In solution it provides the ligand that combines with calcium and magnesium ions to form soluble metal–EDTA complexes.

For detection of the equivalence point, Eriochrome Black T (EBT) is used as indicator. The sample is buffered to about pH 10 with an ammonium hydroxide–ammonium chloride buffer. Under these conditions, hardness ions and EBT form an unstable wine-red metal–indicator complex.

During titration, added EDTA removes Ca²⁺ and Mg²⁺ from the metal–indicator complex by forming the more stable metal–EDTA complex. As long as hardness ions remain, released EBT again combines with them and the wine-red colour persists. When essentially all Ca²⁺ and Mg²⁺ have been complexed by EDTA, the next small excess of EDTA releases the indicator in its blue form. Thus the end point is the sharp change from wine red to blue.

sections.heading: Preparation of solutions for the EDTA method
paragraphs: The textbook first prepares a standard hard-water solution. Pure dry CaCO₃ is dissolved using the minimum required dilute hydrochloric acid, the solution is evaporated to dryness, and the residue is dissolved and diluted so that each millilitre of the final standard hard water corresponds to 1 mg of CaCO₃-equivalent hardness.

The EDTA titrant is prepared from pure EDTA crystals together with a small quantity of MgCl₂ in distilled water. The indicator solution is prepared from Eriochrome Black T in alcohol. The pH-10 buffer is prepared from NH₄Cl and concentrated ammonia and then diluted to the specified volume.

tables.caption: Textbook preparation quantities for the hardness-by-EDTA method
rows: 1.0 g pure, dry CaCO₃; dissolve with minimum dilute HCl, evaporate to dryness, redissolve and make to 1 L; 1 mL corresponds to 1 mg CaCO₃ equivalent
4 g pure EDTA crystals + 0.1 g MgCl₂ in 1 L distilled water
0.5 g Eriochrome Black T in 100 mL alcohol
67.5 g NH₄Cl added to 570 mL concentrated ammonia solution, then diluted to 1 L

sections.heading: Standardisation of EDTA and titration of total hardness
paragraphs: The burette is rinsed and filled with EDTA solution. A 50 mL portion of standard hard water is pipetted into a conical flask; buffer solution and a few drops of EBT are added. The solution is titrated with EDTA until the wine-red colour changes to clear blue. Let the EDTA volume be \(V_1\) mL.
For the unknown sample, 50 mL of the water is treated in the same way and titrated to the same wine-red-to-blue end point. Let this EDTA volume be \(V_2\) mL.

Since 50 mL of the standard hard water contains 50 mg CaCO₃ equivalent, \(V_1\) mL of EDTA corresponds to 50 mg CaCO₃ equivalent. This relation is used to convert the EDTA volume consumed by the unknown sample into hardness.

sections.heading: Permanent hardness and temporary hardness by EDTA
paragraphs: To determine permanent hardness, the textbook takes 250 mL of the sample and boils it until its volume is reduced to about 50 mL. Boiling decomposes bicarbonates and precipitates the temporary-hardness constituents as CaCO₃ and Mg(OH)₂.

The precipitate is filtered off and washed. The filtrate and washings are collected and made back to 250 mL with distilled water. A 50 mL aliquot of this boiled-and-filtered water is then titrated in the same manner with EDTA. Let the EDTA volume be \(V_3\) mL.
The hardness remaining after boiling is permanent hardness. Temporary hardness is obtained by subtracting permanent hardness from total hardness.

sections.heading: Advantages of the EDTA method
paragraphs: The textbook lists three practical advantages of the EDTA method over the older hardness-estimation methods: greater accuracy, convenience and a more rapid procedure.

book_refs.note: Complete EDTA hardness method, calculations and hardness numericals

self_checks.question: What colour change marks the EDTA hardness end point?
How are total and permanent hardness distinguished in the textbook EDTA method?
self_checks.answer: Total hardness is measured directly on the sample; permanent hardness is measured after boiling, filtering and restoring the sample volume. Temporary hardness is total minus permanent hardness.

title: Boiler troubles: scales and sludges
learn: Concentration of dissolved salts during steam generation can produce sludge or scale inside boilers.
Sludge is soft, loose and non-adherent; scale is hard and adherent.
Scale causes serious heat-transfer, fuel-consumption, maintenance, safety and efficiency problems.

sections.heading: Scale and sludge formation in boilers
paragraphs: As boiler water is heated and converted into steam, dissolved salts become progressively concentrated. When their concentration exceeds their solubility under boiler conditions, they precipitate on or within the boiler.

A precipitate that remains soft, loose, slimy and non-adherent is termed sludge. Sludge commonly collects in comparatively cooler parts of the boiler and can often be removed by blow-down. A deposit that becomes hard and adheres firmly to the inner boiler surface is termed scale.
The textbook figure contrasts loose precipitate suspended or deposited in water with the hard coating formed directly on the metal surface.

figures.alt: Placeholder for textbook Fig. 1, Scale and sludge in boilers, on textbook page 7.

sections.heading: Disadvantages of sludge formation
paragraphs: The textbook notes that sludge is a poor conductor of heat and therefore wastes fuel. It can settle in narrow or cooler portions of the boiler, obstructing pipes and fittings and interfering with circulation.

Because sludge promotes local accumulation of solids and poor heat transfer, it can also encourage corrosion beneath deposits. Regular blow-down and proper external treatment of feed water are used to limit sludge formation.

sections.heading: Causes of scale formation
paragraphs: The textbook gives several distinct mechanisms by which scale may form. The important point is that different salts become insoluble for different reasons: decomposition, reduced solubility at high temperature, hydrolysis, or formation of very hard silicate deposits.
bullets: Decomposition of bicarbonates: \(\mathrm{Ca(HCO_3)_2 \rightarrow CaCO_3\downarrow + H_2O + CO_2\uparrow}\).
Deposition of calcium sulphate: the solubility of \(\mathrm{CaSO_4}\) decreases at boiler temperatures, so it can precipitate directly as a hard deposit.
Hydrolysis of magnesium salts: dissolved magnesium salts can hydrolyse and precipitate \(\mathrm{Mg(OH)_2}\), contributing to scale.
Silica and silicates: silica may form calcium or magnesium silicate deposits, which are particularly hard and firmly adherent.

sections.heading: Disadvantages of scale formation
paragraphs: Scale has low thermal conductivity. A scale-coated heating surface therefore requires a larger temperature difference to transfer the same quantity of heat. More fuel must be burnt, and the metal beneath the scale may become dangerously overheated.

The textbook lists wastage of fuel, lowering of boiler safety, reduction in boiler efficiency and danger of explosion among the important consequences. Thick scale may also choke passages and interfere with water circulation.

tables.caption: Textbook table: effect of scale thickness on fuel wastage

sections.heading: Prevention of scale and sludge
paragraphs: The textbook separates preventive treatment into external and internal methods. External treatment removes hardness-producing constituents before the water enters the boiler. Internal treatment adds suitable chemicals within the boiler so that scale-forming constituents are converted into harmless, removable or soluble forms.

For R25, the required internal methods are colloidal conditioning, phosphate conditioning and Calgon conditioning. The required external method is ion-exchange softening/demineralisation, covered separately below.

book_refs.note: Boiler scale, sludge, causes and effects

self_checks.question: What is the main physical difference between scale and sludge?
self_checks.answer: Scale is hard and adherent; sludge is soft, loose and non-adherent.

title: Internal treatment of boiler feed water
learn: Colloidal conditioning converts scale-forming matter into loose non-sticky deposits.
Phosphate conditioning precipitates calcium and magnesium as removable phosphate sludge.
Calgon conditioning holds hardness ions in soluble complex form and prevents scale/sludge deposition.

sections.heading: Internal treatment: principle
paragraphs: Internal treatment is carried out by adding suitable chemicals directly to boiler water. The objective is not necessarily to remove every dissolved salt before it reaches the boiler; instead, scale-forming constituents are converted into forms that remain soluble or form soft, non-adherent sludge that can be removed by blow-down.
R25 specifically requires colloidal, phosphate and Calgon conditioning. These three textbook methods are retained here in the same sequence in which they appear in the chapter.

sections.heading: Colloidal conditioning
paragraphs: For low-pressure boilers, the textbook describes the addition of organic substances such as kerosene, tannin and agar-agar. These substances coat the scale-forming precipitates and change them into loose, non-sticky deposits.

Because the deposits do not adhere firmly to the boiler surface, they can be removed along with boiler water by blow-down. The method is therefore aimed at preventing the formation of a hard adherent scale rather than at eliminating all precipitated matter.

sections.heading: Phosphate conditioning
paragraphs: Phosphate conditioning is described for high-pressure boilers. Sodium phosphate is added so that calcium and magnesium hardness is precipitated as soft phosphate sludge rather than as a hard scale.

The textbook lists three sodium phosphates—sodium dihydrogen phosphate, disodium hydrogen phosphate and trisodium phosphate. Their use is related to the alkalinity of the feed water. The precipitated phosphate sludge remains comparatively non-adherent and can be discharged by blow-down.

sections.heading: Calgon conditioning
paragraphs: Calgon is sodium hexametaphosphate. In water it provides a complex-forming phosphate species that combines with calcium ions. Instead of precipitating as an adherent scale, calcium is held in a soluble complex form.
The textbook therefore presents Calgon conditioning as a way of preventing both scale and sludge formation through complex formation rather than through precipitation.

book_refs.note: Internal treatment methods required by R25

self_checks.question: Which internal treatment uses sodium hexametaphosphate?

title: External treatment: ion-exchange demineralisation
learn: Ion-exchange demineralisation uses synthetic resins containing exchangeable acidic or basic functional groups.
A cation exchanger removes dissolved cations and releases H⁺; an anion exchanger removes dissolved anions and releases OH⁻.
The H⁺ and OH⁻ released in the two stages combine to give water, producing deionised or demineralised water.
Exhausted resins are regenerated and reused.

sections.heading: Ion-exchange or deionisation process
paragraphs: The textbook describes ion exchange as a process using insoluble, cross-linked polymer resins that carry ionisable functional groups. The resins are insoluble in water but can exchange their mobile ions with ions present in the water passing through the bed.

Two types of exchanger are used in sequence. The cation exchanger is used in the hydrogen form and exchanges H⁺ for dissolved metal cations. The anion exchanger is used in the hydroxide form and exchanges OH⁻ for dissolved anions.

sections.heading: Cation-exchange resin
paragraphs: Acidic cation-exchange resins are represented in the textbook by cross-linked aromatic polymers carrying acidic groups such as sulphonic-acid groups. In the hydrogen form, the exchangeable ion is H⁺.

When hard water passes through the cation-exchange column, Ca²⁺, Mg²⁺ and other cations are retained by the resin and an equivalent quantity of H⁺ is released into the water. The dissolved salts are therefore converted into their corresponding acids before the water enters the anion exchanger.

figures.figure_name: Acidic or cation exchange resin (sulphonate form)
figures.alt: Placeholder for textbook Fig. 6, Acidic or cation exchange resin (sulphonate form), on textbook page 17.

sections.heading: Anion-exchange resin
paragraphs: Basic anion-exchange resins contain basic nitrogen-containing functional groups. In the hydroxide form, OH⁻ is the exchangeable ion.

Water leaving the cation exchanger is passed through the anion-exchange column. Chloride, sulphate and other anions are retained on the resin and equivalent OH⁻ ions are released. The H⁺ produced in the first column and the OH⁻ produced in the second combine to form water.

figures.figure_name: Basic or anion exchange resin (hydroxide form)
figures.alt: Placeholder for textbook Fig. 7, Basic or anion exchange resin (hydroxide form), on textbook page 18.

sections.heading: Demineralisation plant
paragraphs: In a two-bed demineralisation unit, raw water first enters the cation-exchange column and then the anion-exchange column. The sequence removes both positively charged and negatively charged dissolved ions.

The textbook notes that the resulting deionised water is essentially free from dissolved ionic salts. The process can produce very low residual hardness and is particularly useful where high-purity water is required.

figures.alt: Placeholder for textbook Fig. 8, Demineralisation of water, on textbook page 19.

sections.heading: Regeneration of exhausted ion exchangers
paragraphs: After continued use, the cation exchanger becomes loaded with metal ions and loses its ability to exchange further H⁺. It is regenerated by passing a dilute mineral acid through the bed, which restores the resin to the hydrogen form and washes the displaced metal ions away.
The anion exchanger becomes loaded with anions and is regenerated with dilute sodium hydroxide, restoring the hydroxide form. After regeneration and washing, the resins can be returned to service.

The textbook also describes a mixed-bed arrangement in which cation and anion resins are mixed for final polishing. During regeneration the two resins are separated, regenerated individually and then remixed.

figures.alt: Placeholder for textbook Fig. 9, Regeneration of mixed-bed ion exchanger, on textbook page 20.

sections.heading: Advantages and limitations noted in the textbook
paragraphs: The textbook emphasises the very high degree of softening obtainable by ion exchange and its suitability for producing demineralised water. It also notes that the equipment is compact and the process can be operated continuously with regeneration cycles.

At the same time, feed containing turbidity or suspended matter can foul or block the resin bed, so pretreatment may be required. The cost of the resin and chemicals for regeneration must also be considered.

self_checks.question: What ions are released by the cation and anion exchangers?
self_checks.answer: The cation exchanger releases H⁺; the anion exchanger releases OH⁻.

title: Potable water and municipal treatment
learn: Municipal treatment converts raw natural water into water suitable for drinking by removing suspended matter, colloidal matter and microorganisms.
The textbook sequence includes screening, sedimentation, coagulation, filtration and disinfection.
Chlorination is explained in detail, including the chemistry of hypochlorous acid and the meaning of break-point chlorination.

sections.heading: Drinking or municipal water: requirements
paragraphs: The textbook defines drinking or potable water as water suitable for safe consumption. It should be clear and odourless, pleasant in taste, reasonably cool and free from disease-producing microorganisms and objectionable dissolved gases.

It also gives numerical limits for several constituents. R25 labels this syllabus point as WHO specifications; the supplied textbook presents the numerical values as drinking-water requirements without explicitly identifying the table as WHO. The values below therefore retain the textbook attribution rather than relabelling them.

tables.caption: Drinking-water values stated in the supplied textbook

sections.heading: Sequence of municipal-water treatment
paragraphs: Natural water from rivers, lakes and other surface sources can contain suspended solids, colloidal particles, dissolved impurities and microorganisms. The textbook treats municipal purification as a sequence in which coarse and settleable matter are removed first, finer suspended and colloidal matter are removed next, and microorganisms are destroyed at the final disinfection stage.
The main stages corresponding to the R25 syllabus are screening, sedimentation, coagulation, filtration and chlorination.

sections.heading: Screening and sedimentation
paragraphs: Screening removes larger floating and suspended impurities by passing raw water through screens. This protects the later treatment units from coarse debris.

After screening, water is allowed to stand in sedimentation tanks. Heavier suspended particles settle under gravity. The textbook notes that sedimentation is much more effective for larger particles than for very fine colloidal material, which remains dispersed because of its small particle size and electrical charge.

sections.heading: Coagulation
paragraphs: When very fine suspended and colloidal particles do not settle readily, a coagulant is added. Coagulation destroys the stability of the colloidal dispersion and produces larger gelatinous flocs. These flocs entrap or adsorb fine impurities and can then settle more readily.

The textbook discusses alum and sodium aluminate as common coagulants. Alum forms a gelatinous aluminium-hydroxide precipitate in the presence of natural alkalinity; this floc sweeps suspended and colloidal matter from the water. Sodium aluminate can also produce aluminium hydroxide and is useful where suitable alkalinity conditions are maintained.

sections.heading: Filtration through a sand filter
paragraphs: After sedimentation and coagulation, water is filtered to remove remaining fine suspended matter and a large proportion of microorganisms. The textbook illustrates a sand filter consisting of graded filtering material through which the water percolates.

As water passes through the filter bed, suspended particles are retained in the voids and on the surfaces of the filter media. Filtration therefore improves clarity and reduces the microbial load before the water reaches the disinfection stage.

figures.alt: Placeholder for textbook Fig. 10, Sand filter, on textbook page 21.

sections.heading: Disinfection by chlorination
paragraphs: The textbook describes chlorination as a widely used method for destroying disease-producing microorganisms. When chlorine is added to water, it hydrolyses to form hydrochloric acid and hypochlorous acid. Hypochlorous acid can dissociate further to hydrogen ion and hypochlorite ion.

The disinfecting action is attributed mainly to hypochlorous acid, which is a stronger germicide than the hypochlorite ion. The relative amounts of these species depend on pH, so the efficiency of chlorination changes with the pH of the water.

Chlorine must be mixed thoroughly with the water and allowed sufficient contact time. The textbook also discusses the importance of maintaining a small residual chlorine concentration after the chlorine demand of the water has been satisfied.

figures.alt: Placeholder for textbook Fig. 11, Chlorinator, on textbook page 23.

sections.heading: Break-point chlorination
paragraphs: Raw water may contain reducing substances, organic matter and ammonia that consume added chlorine. At low chlorine dose, the added chlorine is first used up by these chlorine-demanding substances, so little or no free residual chlorine appears.

With further addition, chlorine reacts with ammonia and nitrogenous material to form chloramines. As the dose is increased still further, these combined-chlorine compounds are oxidised and destroyed, causing the residual chlorine concentration to fall.

A minimum is eventually reached. This point is the break point. Beyond it, further chlorine addition produces a steadily increasing free residual chlorine concentration. The textbook recommends chlorination beyond the break point so that the water receives effective disinfection and retains a protective free-chlorine residual.

figures.alt: Placeholder for textbook Fig. 12, Break-point chlorination curve, on textbook page 24.

sections.heading: Overall drinking-water treatment plant
paragraphs: The chapter concludes the municipal-treatment discussion with a flow diagram that places the principal operations in sequence. The figure is retained as a placeholder for the image pass so that the final page can reproduce the textbook treatment flow visually as well as in text.

self_checks.question: What is break-point chlorination?
self_checks.answer: It is the stage at which chlorine demand has been satisfied and further chlorine addition begins to produce a free residual chlorine concentration.

title: Membrane separation and reverse osmosis
learn: R25 explicitly requires MF, UF and NF membrane types, their advantages and applications.
The supplied Jain & Jain pages do not contain those MF/UF/NF subsections.
The textbook does directly cover reverse osmosis for desalination of brackish or saline water.

sections.heading: Membrane-separation topics required by R25 but absent from supplied textbook pages
paragraphs: R25 explicitly requires the types of membranes Microfiltration (MF), Ultrafiltration (UF) and Nanofiltration (NF), together with their advantages and applications. These three membrane classifications were not found in the supplied Jain & Jain Unit-I pages.

Because this page is being kept textbook-grounded, no outside description of MF, UF or NF has been inserted. They remain a clearly marked source gap until an approved source or class material is supplied.

sections.heading: Desalination of brackish water: reverse osmosis
paragraphs: Desalination means removal of dissolved salts from saline or brackish water. The textbook discusses several desalination methods, but for R25 the required method is reverse osmosis.

In ordinary osmosis, solvent tends to pass through a semipermeable membrane from the dilute side towards the more concentrated side. If a pressure greater than the osmotic pressure is applied to the concentrated saline side, the direction of solvent flow is reversed. Water is forced through the membrane while most dissolved salts are retained. This is reverse osmosis.

The textbook describes pressure being applied to saline water in a reverse-osmosis cell. The membrane separates the feed into a purified-water stream and a more concentrated reject stream. Suitable semipermeable membranes are therefore the key component of the process.

figures.alt: Placeholder for textbook Fig. 17, Reverse osmosis cell, on textbook page 27.

sections.heading: Advantages of reverse osmosis listed in the textbook
paragraphs: The textbook lists several practical advantages of reverse osmosis: the process is comparatively simple, can operate continuously, requires relatively little space, and avoids the large thermal-energy requirement of evaporation-based desalination.

It also notes comparatively low operating cost, reliability and the ability to remove dissolved salts without a phase change of the water. These features make reverse osmosis suitable for producing usable water from brackish or saline feed.

cautions: MF, UF and NF remain an explicit source gap until an approved source is supplied.

self_checks.question: What pressure condition is required for reverse osmosis?
self_checks.answer: An applied pressure greater than the osmotic pressure on the concentrated/saline side.
